title: Runtime feature flagging and experimentation contract
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview
--------
This document defines the architecture and operational contract for feature flagging and experimentation that touches the serving runtime. It covers how runtime-visible flags are declared, negotiated with kernels, staged in production, instrumented for SLO-aware rollouts, and automatically (or manually) rolled back. It is intended for runtime engineers, release engineers, kernel maintainers, and SREs who operate inference fleets.

Scope
-----
- Applies to any toggle that changes runtime execution behavior: kernel selection, batching policy, KV cache semantics, prefetch hints, quantization/fast-path heuristics, backpressure thresholds, admission controls, and routing fallbacks.
- Excludes UI-only feature flags, SDK developer flags, or experiment flags that do not alter server-side execution.

Goals
-----
1. Provide a single, auditable contract for staging and running runtime-facing feature flags.
2. Ensure rollouts are SLO-aware with automated safety gates that prevent expensive regressions.
3. Standardize telemetry and decision tracing so every flag decision can be reconstructed end-to-end.
4. Reduce blast radius with progressive targeting (canary -> ramp -> percent -> full) and deterministic fallback strategies.

Key definitions
---------------
- Flag: An identifier that toggles behavior in the runtime (e.g., runtime.kv_prefetch_v2).
- Kernel capability: a runtime or accelerator property (e.g., async_prefetch, sharded_attention_v2) that a kernel exposes and can negotiate with the control plane.
- Decision trace: structured metadata attached to each request that records the flag decisions and kernel choices used to serve the request.
- Safety gate: a set of observable constraints (SLO/metric thresholds) that must hold before a flag can progress to the next stage.

Contract: Flag lifecycle and metadata
------------------------------------
Every runtime flag must have the following canonical metadata (stored in the feature-store):
- id: short dashed name, e.g., runtime.kv_prefetch_v2
- owner: GitHub handle and team, e.g., @asha / runtime-kernels
- description: one-sentence purpose and risk summary
- scope: one of [kernel-level, node-level, tenant-level, route-level]
- default: boolean (sane production default)
- stages: ordered list: [canary, ramp, percent, full, deprecated]
- canary_policy: YAML pointer to rollout policy (see examples)
- telemetry_keys: list of required metrics and trace attributes (see Observability section)
- precondition_checks: optional list of checks (e.g., min-gpu-firmware-version, kvcache-available)
- rollback_policy: pointer to automated rollback rule set
- audit_log_url: URL to changelog / PR for the flag

Example metadata (YAML snippet for the feature-store):
```
id: runtime.kv_prefetch_v2
owner: @asha (runtime-kernels)
description: Enable asynchronous KV prefetching for seed-based warmup to reduce cold tail latency. Risk: may increase memory churn under high-concurrency workloads.
scope: node-level
default: false
stages: [canary, ramp, percent, full]
canary_policy: /flags/policies/canary-kv-prefetch-v2.yaml
telemetry_keys: [p50, p95, p99, cpu_util, gpu_mem_used, kv_prefetch_hit_ratio]
precondition_checks: [gpu_driver>=560.20, kvcache_enabled]
rollback_policy: /flags/rollback/auto-sla-rollback.yaml
audit_log_url: https://sc/reviews/12345
```

Runtime negotiation and kernel capability model
----------------------------------------------
1. Capability declaration: Each kernel binary declares a static capability vector at build time (JSON manifest attached to the runtime image). Capabilities are short tokens: async_prefetch, sharded_attn_v2, quant_fp8_fastpath.
2. Dynamic negotiation: At node start, the control plane retrieves the capability vector and stores it with node metadata. Flags scoped to kernel-level are only eligible for nodes that advertise the required capability.
3. Fallback compatibility matrix: For each flag, authors must provide a fallback kernel variant or a safe no-op. Control plane enforces that flag activation never routes traffic to an incompatible kernel.

Example kernel manifest (single-line JSON for feature-store):
{"kernel_version":"3.2.0","capabilities":["async_prefetch","sharded_attn_v2"]} 

Canary and rollout policy (SLO-aware)
-------------------------------------
All rollout policies must include: target traffic fraction, duration, ramp step size, observation window, and safety gates. Safety gates are specified as PromQL-style constraints.

Minimum canary policy (example):
```
name: kv-prefetch-v2-canary
target_fraction: 0.01 # 1% of signed traffic
duration: 2h
steps:
  - until: 30m
    fraction: 0.01
  - until: 1h
    fraction: 0.05
observation_window: 5m
safety_gates:
  - name: p99-latency-regression
    query: rate(p99_latency_ms[5m]) > baseline_p99 * 1.15
  - name: cpu-spike
    query: avg(cpu_user_seconds_total[5m]) > baseline_cpu * 1.2
```
Progression rules: a step only advances when none of the safety gates have fired for two consecutive observation windows. If any gate fires, follow rollback policy.

Telemetry and decision tracing requirements
-----------------------------------------
Every request served under a runtime flag must record the following trace attributes (as structured tags):
- flag.id (string)
- flag.stage (canary|ramp|percent|full)
- kernel.id
- kernel.capabilities (comma-separated token list)
- decision.reason (e.g., 'canary-match','tenant-override','precondition-fail')
- decision.timestamp (ISO8601)
- fallback.used (true|false)

Required aggregated metrics (per-flag and per-kernel) reported at 1m resolution:
- request_count
- successful_count
- error_rate (5xx / total)
- latency_p50_ms, latency_p95_ms, latency_p99_ms
- cpu_util_percent
- gpu_mem_bytes_used
- kv_prefetch_hit_ratio (when applicable)
- cost_per_1000_tokens (est.)

Observability dashboards and baseline generation
------------------------------------------------
- Every flag must have a templated dashboard generated automatically (Flag Overview): timeline of rollout fraction, p50/p95/p99, error_rate, resource usage, and decision_trace sampling panel.
- Baselines: rollouts must compare to a running baseline captured from the 72h window before the rollout. Baseline values are stored in the experiment index and used in safety gate expressions.
- Example PromQL safety gate (p99 regression):
  (avg_over_time(latency_p99_ms{flag=\"control\"}[72h]) * 1.15) < avg_over_time(latency_p99_ms{flag=\"candidate\"}[5m])

Automated rollback and escalation
--------------------------------
Two rollback mechanisms are supported: automated rollback and manual rollback. Authors must declare which mechanism applies and provide the thresholds.

Automated rollback rule template (example):
- Trigger: any safety gate that is marked auto-rollback triggers immediate rollback.
- Action: flag is set to previous stage (or disabled if canary) and affected traffic is re-routed to fallback kernel.
- Notification: paging to on-call + slack #runtime-incidents + email to flag owner and reviewers.

Manual rollback: Any engineer can manually revert via the feature-store UI or CLI; manual rollback must include reason and a summary to the audit log.

Experimentation harness and synthetic traffic protocol
-----------------------------------------------------
We require a reproducible synthetic load generator for each flag to exercise worst-case shapes (short bursts, long-context, many small parallel requests). The harness must:
- Support tenant-scoped replay with recording/replay of real traffic signatures (scrubbed for PII)
- Provide pre-seeded KV cache patterns and long/short sequence distributions
- Allow failure injection (GPU OOM, NVLink latency, kernel timeouts) to test fallback behavior

Commands (example):
- Start a canary run: `rx experiment start --flag runtime.kv_prefetch_v2 --policy kv-prefetch-v2-canary`
- Attach synthetic traffic: `rx loadgen --profile long-context-burst --tenants 100 --qps 200`
- Collect traces: `rx traces export --filter flag=runtime.kv_prefetch_v2 --since 60m`

Kernel rollout considerations
---------------------------
- Kernel authors must include a compatibility shim that allows a node to accept both old and new kernels during a rolling upgrade.
- Rolling kernel upgrades must be coordinated with flag rollouts: a flag that depends on a new kernel capability must not be advanced beyond canary until 80% of eligible nodes are on the target kernel.
- If the target capability is optional (best-effort), flag authors must specify safe degradation path in the metadata.

SLOs and alerting thresholds (suggested defaults)
--------------------------------------------------
These thresholds are minimums; product teams may tighten them for higher-risk flags. All alerts are aggregated by flag and by model/route.
- Error rate increase: > 0.5 percentage point absolute increase over baseline (5m window)
- p95 latency increase: > baseline_p95 * 1.20 (5m window)
- p99 latency increase: > baseline_p99 * 1.10 (5m window)
- CPU usage: sustained > baseline * 1.25 (10m)
- GPU memory pressure: > 85% for any node (1m)
- Cost per 1k tokens: > baseline * 1.3 (24h)

Runbook: immediate steps when a safety gate fires
------------------------------------------------
1. Alert fires -> page on-call SRE and notify flag owner.
2. On-call runs `rx flags status --id runtime.kv_prefetch_v2` to confirm active stage.
3. If auto-rollback enabled, verify whether rollback already executed. If not, run `rx flags rollback --id runtime.kv_prefetch_v2 --reason \"auto_gate_fire_manual_confirm\"`.
4. If manual rollback required, set flag to previous stage and re-route traffic.
5. Collect artifacts: 1m-resolution metrics, 1000 sampled traces (decision traces), kernel logs from nodes in cohort, and synthetic harness logs.
6. Postmortem: owner opens a short incident review within 48h, including root cause hypothesis and next steps.

Ownership and approvals
-----------------------
- Flag owner (declared in metadata) is responsible for: precondition checks, telemetry coverage, and runbook artifacts.
- Kernel owners must sign off on capability declarations and provide fallback readiness proof.
- Release owner (release-engineering) must approve any global >10% traffic ramp.
- Security review required for any flag that changes encryption, key usage, or telemetry collection.

Implementation examples
-----------------------
Feature-store CLI example (create a flag):
```
rx flags create --id runtime.kv_prefetch_v2 \
  --owner @asha --scope node-level --default false \
  --telemetry p99,kv_prefetch_hit_ratio,cpu_util --precondition kvcache_enabled
```

Prometheus rule example (p99 regression gate):
```
alert: Flag_P99_Regression
expr: (avg_over_time(latency_p99_ms{flag=\"candidate\"}[5m]) > avg_over_time(latency_p99_ms{flag=\"control\"}[72h]) * 1.15)
for: 2m
labels:
  severity: page
annotations:
  summary: \"Candidate p99 exceeding baseline by >15%\"
```

Change log and auditability
---------------------------
- Every state transition (create, canary-start, ramp-step, rollback, disable) must be recorded in the audit log with: user, timestamp, previous_state, new_state, reason, and a link to the PR/change.
- Audit retention: 3 years for production-facing flags.

Security and privacy notes
--------------------------
- Decision traces must not contain PII. Fields that could contain user data must be hashed or replaced with stable pseudonyms.
- Experiment replay must use scrubbed recordings: scrub policy stored at /policies/replay-scrub-policy.md

Appendix: FAQ and common patterns
----------------------------------
Q: When should a flag be kernel-level vs node-level?
A: Kernel-level flags are for behavior inside kernel code paths that are compiled-in; node-level for runtime orchestration or config toggles. If the change touches GPU kernel binary interfaces, use kernel-level.

Q: Can we bypass the safety gates for urgent hotfixes?
A: Only with a documented emergency exemption approved by Release Engineering + SRE. The exemption must be recorded and the flag reverted to standard flow within 24h.
